title: I made 2 games without AI. Now I'm vibe coding my third game, and here's what I've learned.
author: dedaistgeil
selftext:
Hey everyone, grab yourself a drink and get comfortable. This might be a longer one.

I'm Deda, a solo indie dev from germany, and over the past 2 years I've created two games completely without AI. Now I'm working on my third game, but this time I'm trying something completely different: going all in on vibe coding**.**

I wanted to share my experience so far, especially because I think there's a pretty big misconception about how easy it actually is to make a good game with AI.

But first, a little background.

**My first game: What Is The Ghost**

My first game is called [What Is The Ghost](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3929260/What_Is_The_Ghost/). It's a 2D ghost hunting game inspired by Phasmophobia. It took me over a year to finish, and oh boy, implementing multiplayer was a crazy amount of work.I made pretty much everything myself, except for the soundtrack in the main menu, which was actually created by one of my viewers.

The game has made roughly $2.5k in net revenue so far. Nothing life changing, but I'm happy with what I've acomplished, especially considering how much I learned along the way.

**My second game: Capy Farm**

For my second game, [Capy Farm](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4849560/Capy_Farm/), I wanted to challenge myself to develop something as quickly as possible. So I bought an asset pack, looked into what makes incremental games fun, and started developing (never played an incremental game myself before). After just 1,5 months, the game was basically finished, with only some polishing left to do. It's currently participating in Steam Next Fest and sitting at around 800 wishlists. The release is planned for November 2nd.

Both games were developed without AI, and I know pretty much every corner of my codebase to this day.

**Now comes game number 3, and my brother is partially to blame for this one.**

My brother absolutely LOVES AI and vibe coding. For months, he kept telling me to give it a try. And my response was always something like:

*"No bro, I want to have complete control over my games. If something breaks, I want to know exactly where to look in my code and how to fix it."*

Remember that sentence. We'll come back to it. So here I am, thinking about my third game, and I finally decided to give it a shot. This time, I'm going all in on AI, using GPT Codex with my Plus subscription for basically the entire development process. I came up with a concept, wrote my first prompt, and suddenly I had a playable prototype. 

Pretty crazy, right?

I won't go into the details of the game itself because I want to keep my handcrafted games and my AI developed projects separate. I also plan to be transparent about AI usage and clearly disclose it. But after spending some time working on this third game, I've learned quite a few things about vibe coding and the infamous **"**AI Slop**"** discussion.

Before starting, I genuinely thought AI had become so good that you could create a polished game with very little time and effort.

Well, turns out it's not that simple.

**1. Creating a playable game is surprisingly easy**

This is honestly the most impressive part. You describe what you want, give the AI some instructions, and within a relatively short time you can have something playable. Something that would have taken me days or even weeks to build manually can sometimes be prototyped much faster. That's absolutely crazy, especially as a solo developer.

But there's one important thing people on each side of the AI Slop debate:

A playable prototype, unpolished slop and a finished, good game are VERY different things.

And that brings me to my next point.

**2. Polishing is where the real work begins**

Dude... Once you have your playable prototype, you start noticing all the little things that aren't quite right. The UI feels weird. Some textures don't fit together. Animations look off. The environment feels empty. Performance could be better. The gameplay works, but something about it just isn't fun yet. And the more you look, the more things you find. 

UI, 3D assets, textures, lore, environment design, balancing, performance, sound design, game feel. There's always something. AI can help with many of these things, but it doesn't automatically know what makes your game feel good. You still need to make decisions, test things, iterate a lot if times, and sometimes completely rework what the AI created. And just because the code runs without errors doesn't mean the gameplay is actually fun.

AI makes it easier to create something. It doesn't automatically make that something worth playing.

**3. I was right about wanting control over my code (unfortunately)**

Remember what I told my brother? Yeah... This is probably my biggest personal struggle with vibe coding so far. As someone who normally builds everything himself, I'm used to knowing exactly how my game works. If a button needs to be moved, I know where to go. If a mechanic breaks, I usually have a pretty good idea where the problem is.

But now?

Sometimes I want to change the most basic thing, and I have absolutely no idea where to start. Either because I'm unfamiliar with the engine or because I simply didn't write the code myself. So I go back to the AI and ask it to make the change. And sometimes it works perfectly. Other times it fixes one thing and accidentally breaks something else. Then I need another prompt to fix that. And another one. You get the idea. I never expected to feel this dependent on a tool that was supposed to make development easier. It's teaching me that even when using AI, understanding your project structure and reviewing the generated code is still incredibly valuable. Otherwise, you might end up with a game that works, but you have no idea how to maintain it.

**4. What actually separates "AI Slop" from a good game?**

This is probably the most interesting lesson for me. I see a lot of people calling AI games "AI Slop", and to be fair, I understand where some of that criticism comes from. But I don't think using AI automatically makes a game bad. In my opinion, a good game is a fun, polished experience where you can tell that someone actually cared about the end result. And I think that's exactly what a lot of the games labeled as "AI Slop" are missing. Not necessarily because AI was used, but because there wasn't enough work put into turning the generated output into something cohesive and enjoyable. Of course, polishing alone won't save a boring game. You still need a good concept, interesting mechanics, a consistent art direction, and most importantly, something that makes people want to keep playing. But that's kind of my point. AI can generate code, assets, and ideas. It can speed up development tremendously.

**But it doesn't replace having a vision for your game or knowing what makes it good.**

You still need someone making the decisions. Someone who notices when things feel wrong. Someone who actually cares enough to keep improving the game instead of shipping the first thing that works.

And I think that's where the difference is.

**5. My biggest takeaway so far**

I used to think vibe coding was basically a shortcut to making games. Now I see it more as a different way of developing them, with its own advantages and frustrations. The barrier to creating a playable prototype has become incredibly low. But the barrier to creating a genuinely good game? I'm not convinced that has changed nearly as much. You still need creativity, patience, testing, and a lot of iteration. And ironically, the more experience you already have as a developer, the easier it seems to recognize when the AI is doing something stupid. I definitely don't regret trying it, though. It's fascinating to see what's possible, and I'm curious how far I can take this third project. Maybe I'll end up loving this workflow. Maybe I'll go back to writing everything myself. Maybe I'll find a balance somewhere in between. For now, I'm just experimenting and learning.

**6. I feel like my coding skills are getting rusty**

This one actually bothers me quite a bit. I've developed two complete games without AI. I used to write everything myself, solve problems on my own, and figure things out through trial and error. But now that I'm relying so much on AI, I'm noticing something I didn't really expect. 

I'm slowly getting worse at doing things myself.

Sometimes I catch myself struggling with things that used to be pretty straightforward for me. Instead of thinking about how to implement something, my first instinct is to just ask AI to do it. And honestly, that's a little scary. It's not like I've suddenly forgotten how to code, but I can definitely feel myself getting rusty. Things that used to come naturally now require more thinking, simply because I'm not practicing them as much anymore. It's also incredibly tempting to take the easy route. Why spend 30 minutes figuring something out when AI can potentially do it in 30 seconds?

I'm becoming faster at getting things done, but potentially worse at doing them myself.

And as someone who genuinely enjoys programming, that's something I don't want to lose. Maybe the solution is to keep it like I said fully handcrafted games and Vibe-Coded games. So every now and then I can feel the satisfaction of handcrafting a game and keep my skills.

**Anyway, I'm curious about your experiences.**

How long does it usually take you to go from a playable prototype to a game you actually feel comfortable releasing? And do you agree that polishing and having a clear creative vision are what separate "AI Slop" from good games? Or do you think there's more to it? 

Would love to hear some perspectives.

\--------

**TL;DR:** I'm a solo indie dev who made two games without AI and decided to go all in on vibe coding for my third. Creating a playable prototype with AI is surprisingly easy, but turning it into a polished, fun game still takes a ton of work. I also struggle with losing control over my own code and have noticed my programming skills getting rusty because I rely on AI so much.

My biggest takeaway? **AI makes it easier than ever to create a game, but making a GOOD game still requires skill, creativity, and a lot of polishing.**

comments.author: the_builder_ai
comments.body: 100% agree on your point "AI makes it easier than ever to create a game, but making a GOOD game still requires skill, creativity, and a lot of polishing," the combination of 2 and 4. I think people point out "AI Slop" because a lot of people just one prompt build and show the product but I also found out that the most simple things take the most work with AI. For example, move this UI a bit to left - how much is a bit? It is easy with human to make judgment but with AI it is not as straightforward. Tiny things like something facing the wrong direction or wrong placement jumps out.

replies.author: dedaistgeil
replies.body: Yes it's very hard to be precise, that's where I miss the control of a completely handcrafted game.

comments.author: Dicethrower
comments.body:
From personal experience I agree with almost everything. I think the really big take away is exactly these words:

>It doesn't replace having a vision for your game or knowing what makes it good.

This is why I'm not worried about AI replacing jobs, or flooding the market. We've always had crappy games even before AI. Devs that get how this industry actually works are going to thrive now.

replies.author: dedaistgeil
replies.body:
Yes being a game dev is still rewarding and can build a future. AI is just another tool that makes it easier to enter game development. It is a powerful tool in the correct hands. 

The only point at which AI would be a threat is when people actually start liking bad games. That's when we are doomed.

comments.author: Rogetec
comments.body:
I learned that too. I do try AI to make a game, but... unless you just go for blatant copy (as often is the case with many AI games/AI demos we see on reddit), it's not so easy.

You have to write down systems, what you want... you need to have things organized before you start pumping out the content. You can't just go on with content and game without them, because your game will end up being flat and "interesting" parts will be just boring flat stat boosts.

Not to mention optimization part; it also needs help. Of course AI helps a lot, but still - AI sometimes won't notice performance issues, unless you point it out and want AI to check in this direction.

So yeah, you need to have ideas in your head. AI can make stuff correct on 1st or 2nd time - but you cannot count on AI making everything perfectly every single time - especially when it comes to system, satisfying progression, good balance (so you don't steamroll game or get stuck for a long time in one spot)...

I appreciate AI and it helps a lot, but at the same time it shows you need things figured out. Need to know how to name art styles, what colors, fonts for UI etc. You need to know your things if you try to make something original.
